p.x:
My video on The Screen of Consciousness in brief essay form:

--

Introduction: The Strange Ubiquity of “The Inner Screen”

Close your eyes, open them again, and notice how the scene simply is there: colors co-present with edges, bodily sensations quietly co-occupying the same psychological theatre, thoughts and emotions woven through in a collage of qualia values. Philosophers call this the phenomenological screen of consciousness: a field where disparate data appear simultaneously, owned by one subject, without seams or loading bars.  Daniel Dennett’s-famous Multiple Drafts model invites us to treat that seamlessness as a useful narrative, stitched together only when we query it. Perhaps. But even if every stream is perpetually “edited in post,” the model still owes us an account of how, at the decisive moment of query, an integrated gestalt can crystallise out of trillions of neuronal micro-events. The essay presses on precisely that puzzle by interrogating the most common metaphor enlisted to explain it: the mind as a camera projecting its own private movie.

Does the Screen of Consciousness Work as a Camera?

At first pass the idea feels irresistible. Sense data arrive from “outside,” a biological lens funnels them through a neural aperture, and somewhere deeper (a thalamic or cortical CCD, perhaps) a picture forms. Voilà: a private cinema in which the self sits as silent spectator.  Yet the closer we examine this camera analogy, the faster it buckles under its own optics.

A literal pin-hole has no area and therefore no space to bind anything. The most it could carry is a single brightness value, while a conscious instant expresses gigabits of coloured, textured, valenced structure.  Widen the aperture to capture that richness and the metaphor stumbles into classical physics: any extended patch of brain can be partitioned ad infinitum. Why should exactly this two-millimetre blob of V1, and not 1.8 mm or 2.2 mm, constitute the observing subject?  Nothing in an atoms-and-forces ontology privileges one carving over another; unity becomes a projection of the theorist, not a property of the substrate.

Perhaps, then, the binding happens on the sensor, the putative “screen” of neural pixels. But a million independent photodiodes still need an integrator to read them out and weave a gestalt. Drafting a new homunculus merely pushes the problem back a level... an infinite stairwell of cameras observing cameras.  Reject the homunculus and you are left with a swarm of locally interacting detectors that, by ordinary causality, have no path to the holistic cross-talk our phenomenology undeniably exhibits. Optics sharpens the critique: the Rayleigh limit demands an aperture larger than the finest detail it resolves, reinstating the extended-region dilemma instead of solving it.

The deeper issue is that the camera picture carries set-theoretic assumptions (world-as-points, causality-as-neighbour-interactions) into a domain where those assumptions fail.  Moments of consciousness act like topologically individuated, globally phase-coupled wholes: simultaneously one and many. Classical mechanics can approximate functional integration (the behavioural ability to coordinate inputs) but it cannot mint the felt unity in which all that content appears at once for someone. Cellular automata, for instance, harbour “gliders” and other patterns, yet every pattern’s boundary is chosen by an outside observer; nothing in the substrate forces a clean cut that would ground a cohesive subject. The cellular automaton's behavior and ontology is fully specified by the local interactions, with no observer-independent wholes.

What does fit the data is a family of counter-metaphors rooted in holistic physics. An optical cavity lets light bounce until a standing wave emerges whose mode structure cannot be reduced to individual reflections.  Twist a balloon and two lobes share a single pinch-point; cross that bottleneck and local information vanishes, effectively sealing each lobe into its own causal domain. Or consider a quantum path integral: every possible trajectory interferes, cancelling most while summing a few into the amplitude we observe. In each case unity-and-multiplicity coexist as a primitive, not as an assembly job done inside a hidden lens.

Seen through that lens (heh) the camera analogy reveals more about our deep seated need for pictorial shortcuts than about the nature of mind. A faithful account of the “screen of consciousness” will almost certainly invoke field-level phase coupling, topological segmentation, and superposed dynamics that treat wholes as basic, or at least something with a "flavor" that allows for true "wholes". Until then, the internal camera remains a clever prop whose aperture admits just enough light to show why it cannot possibly work.

p.x:
Assume that everybody on Earth got access to a genie. The genie is able to give any wish that is physically possible. All it asks for in return is to provide it with sufficient energy somehow that it can function. It's not really a problem because genies can make their own energy but you know that's the contract. If it can't suffice you need to give it or it stops working.

Let's examine the equilibrium. The genie is a universal transformer and gets us a flat production function - post-scarcity for ordinary goods, not for everything.

First all demands from our "demandscape" can get satisfied. Most supply chains and current economics will collapse, because you no longer need companies to provide you with things. You don't need machines when you have a genie. You don't need industrial organization either. 

So what remains scarce? Numeraire (energy, materials) and positional goods. So what if there's adversarial "demands"? The genies can fight with each other. Now the energy demands can come to fore a bit more, because any marginal requirement is something you have to provide. This is a more Hobbesian world.

The energy needs are, let's say, satisfiable with the usual power plant/ nuclear/ solar. Land to cover with solar arrays becomes the core thing to fight over. Or materials to make nuclear power. Or to make chips, or the future chip equivalents. We mine asteroids, make dyson swarms, whatever.

But until we find zero point energy that makes this problem also disappear, we have another resource to fight over. But back to the economics, for basically almost no cost we have provided for a large chunk of what people want in their lives. In this place what does ownership mean. 

What about property rights? Could people in any meaningful sense own a Dyson swarm? Especially if others also have a genie with which they can if not compel to transfer ownership at least destroy? What would blackmailing look like in such a world. Property only matters insofar as enforcement is possible. Would governments tax genies, and keep a genie army?

More importantly if you have more genies than others, you can possibly create things that they would like to purchase from you. Some things are of course easier to recreate the second time which makes status competition to be first and most creative something to fight over. Also, creates a financial industry for some to "borrow" genies to pay back later. Time and social rank can't be produced.

Even with a perfectly magical genie we'd find a way to recreate wall street and silicon valley, because human demandscape isn't unidimensional. If genies aren't costless we'll see the emergence of finance and tech and trade.

So, the equilibria;
1. A Hobbesian world where we have low trust, high property fragility, shrunken trade
2. MAD and treaties and trade: similar in some ways to intl. treaties and trade today

At the end of all of this we still assume humans know what to ask for so the genies can provide it. Or do we outsource that to genies too? Like wireheading but worse? Some might, I already ask LLMs where to eat, but I'm the one asking. 

Given universal production + universal destruction, the binding choice variable is institutional design. More on this all through 2026.
